plan.contextChunk: This figure places three small sketched graphs side by side, labeled (a), (b), and (c), each showing curves that rise from left to right on an unmarked vertical axis above a horizontal axis whose tip is labeled n; no numeric ticks appear anywhere. Panel (a) carries three curves: the highest is labeled c2 g(n), the lowest c1 g(n), and a third labeled f(n) weaves between them, dipping and crossing near the left edge before settling into the corridor between the other two. A dashed vertical segment drops from that crossing region to a tick on the n axis marked n0, and the expression f(n) = Theta(g(n)) is printed below the plot. Panel (b) has two curves, the upper labeled c g(n) and the lower labeled f(n); f(n) oscillates sharply at small n, meets c g(n) at the dashed line standing over the tick n0, and runs beneath it from there on, with f(n) = O(g(n)) underneath. Panel (c) reverses the roles, putting f(n) above and c g(n) below after they touch at the dashed n0 line, and is captioned f(n) = Omega(g(n)). Read against one another, the three panels turn on where the labeled curve sits relative to the scaled comparison function once n passes n0, giving the geometric intuition behind bounding a function from both sides, from above only, and from below only.

interactionPlan.concept: Asymptotic notation describes the long-term growth of a function by showing it is eventually bounded above, below, or both by scaled versions of a simpler reference function.
elements: x-axis with arrow and 'n' label
y-axis (unmarked)
Black curve f(n) featuring oscillations at small n, settling into smooth growth
Upper bounding curve c2 g(n) (labeled 'c g(n)' in Big-O mode)
Lower bounding curve c1 g(n) (labeled 'c g(n)' in Big-Omega mode)
Vertical dashed line at n0 dropping to an 'n0' label on the x-axis
Shaded valid region extending rightward from n0 (below upper bound, above lower bound, or between both)
Red violation highlights on segments of f(n) that escape the shaded region for n > n0
Curve labels positioned near their right ends
Formula label below the graph (e.g., 'f(n) = Θ(g(n))')

interactions.label: Bound Type
interactions.teaches: The structural difference between providing only an upper limit (O), only a lower limit (Ω), or sandwiching the function from both sides (Θ).

interactions.label: Threshold (n0)
interactions.teaches: Bounds only need to hold for sufficiently large inputs; sliding n0 left exposes early noise that violates the bounds, illustrating why asymptotic analysis ignores small-input behavior.

interactions.label: Constant Multiplier (c)
interactions.teaches: The exact bounding curves can be scaled by arbitrary constants; tightening the multiplier shows how bounds can squeeze f(n) as long as it remains contained.

demo_steps.title: Big-O: Upper Bound
demo_steps.narration: O-notation defines an upper bound. f(n) = O(g(n)) means there is some constant c such that f(n) is entirely beneath c g(n) for all inputs larger than n0.

demo_steps.title: Big-Omega: Lower Bound
demo_steps.narration: Ω-notation defines a lower bound. f(n) = Ω(g(n)) means f(n) stays above a scaled version of g(n) for all n ≥ n0.

demo_steps.title: Big-Theta: Tight Bound
demo_steps.narration: Θ-notation bounds the function from both sides. f(n) is sandwiched between c1 g(n) and c2 g(n) for all n ≥ n0, meaning f(n) and g(n) grow at the same rate.

demo_steps.title: The role of n0
demo_steps.narration: Move n0 to the left to include small inputs. The early oscillations of f(n) now violate the bounds (marked in red). Asymptotic notation deliberately ignores this early noise.

demo_steps.title: Adjusting constants
demo_steps.narration: The constants c1 and c2 can be adjusted. As long as we can find SOME valid constants that eventually sandwich f(n), the asymptotic bound holds.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Asymptotic bounds do not require a perfect fit everywhere; they only require that scaled versions of a reference function can eventually trap the target function beyond some threshold n0.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Draw a single coordinate system rather than three separate panels, updating its contents based on the toggle. f(n) should be a black curve that oscillates up and down for n < 20, then grows smoothly (e.g., following an n^1.5 trend). g(n) is the smooth reference trend. The cMultiplier slider dictates the bound spacing: upper bound c2 = cMultiplier, lower bound c1 = 1 / cMultiplier. For Big-O, show only the c2 g(n) curve and shade everything below it for n >= n0. For Big-Omega, show only the c1 g(n) curve and shade everything above it for n >= n0. For Big-Theta, show both curves and shade between them. Any segment of f(n) strictly to the right of n0 that falls outside the shaded valid region must be highlighted in thick red. Update the formula label at the bottom (e.g. 'f(n) = O(g(n))') to match the active toggle.

discrepancies: The mathematical labels (e.g., f(n), c g(n)) are rendered in a sans-serif font instead of a serif math font, and the constant multiplier labels include an extra space ('c g(n)' instead of 'cg(n)').

In the source, n₀ is strictly marked at an intersection point and the dashed line stops there; in the interactive figure, n₀ is freely adjustable via slider and its dashed line extends up to the uppermost curve.
A blue shaded region is dynamically drawn for n ≥ n₀ to emphasize the bounded area, which is a pedagogical addition absent in the original static figure.
